subject: Business
title: Diversification: Don't Put All Eggs in One Basket
description: Learn Diversification: Don't Put All Eggs in One Basket in one minute.

hook.text: Enron employees had 62% of their 401(k) in Enron stock. When the company collapsed, they lost their jobs and savings.

buildup.text: Diversification means spreading investments across different assets so no single failure can wipe you out.

discovery.text: A mix of stocks, bonds, real estate, and international investments reduces overall risk without proportionally reducing returns.

twist.text: Over-diversification exists too. Owning 500 stocks gives little additional benefit over 30 well-chosen ones.

climax.text: Nobel laureate Harry Markowitz called diversification 'the only free lunch in finance.' Risk drops, returns hold.

punchline.text: Concentration builds wealth. Diversification protects it.

quiz.question: Why did Harry Markowitz call diversification 'the only free lunch in finance'?
options: It reduces risk without proportionally reducing returns
It guarantees higher returns than any single stock

details.summary: Diversification spreads investments across different asset classes, sectors, and geographies to reduce overall portfolio risk. When one investment declines, others may hold steady or rise, smoothing returns and protecting against catastrophic losses.
details.whyItMatters: Concentration in a single stock or sector exposes you to devastating losses. Diversification is the only free lunch in investing because it reduces risk without necessarily reducing expected returns.
takeaways: Spreading investments across asset classes reduces portfolio volatility
Diversification protects against catastrophic loss from any single investment
True diversification requires assets that do not move in lockstep

faq.question: How many stocks do you need for proper diversification?
faq.answer: Research shows most stock-specific risk is eliminated with 20 to 30 stocks across different sectors. However, index funds holding hundreds or thousands of stocks provide instant broad diversification in a single purchase, which is simpler for most investors.

faq.question: Can you be too diversified?
faq.answer: Over-diversification, or diworsification, can dilute returns to the point where your portfolio essentially matches the market average with higher fees. Holding too many overlapping funds may add complexity and costs without meaningful additional risk reduction.
